label: Differentiability implies continuity
subgoals: Apply: differentiable at a, continuous at a

slice.rule: If $f$ is differentiable at $a$, it is continuous there. The idea behind the proof is that $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} = \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h-a}\cdot 1$ splits into a difference quotient, which stays finite because the derivative exists, times a factor that tends to 1. A finite quantity times something tending to 1 tends to a finite number, and that limit is $f(a+h)-f(a) \to 0$.

examples.says: continuous but not differentiable — the converse fails here

slice.rule: Continuity does not imply differentiability. A corner, a cusp and a vertical tangent all leave the function continuous while destroying the limit of the difference quotient, because the left and right slopes disagree. $f(x)=|x|$ at 0 is the standard example: it is continuous, and the one-sided slopes are $-1$ and $1$.

examples.says: vertical tangent — derivative is infinite, so no finite derivative

slice.note: Undefined and discontinuous are different failures. A corner is defined and continuous; the problem is only the slope.

slice.rule: To test differentiability at a point, compute the difference quotient limit from each side separately. If both exist and agree, the function is differentiable there. If they disagree you have a corner or a cusp; if either side has no limit you do not even have continuity to start from.
